description: REQUIRED whenever you create an account/identity anywhere in the world — a signup, a registration, a service login. Record: service, username, owner ('project' when it hangs off an identity the project owns like its own email/domain; 'chairman' when a responsible human is the name behind it — when unsure, ask in the boardroom), the NAME of the stored credential (never a value — store values as secrets via a need, or note where they live), url, and a note with what matters at wind-down (plan tier, renewal date, how to cancel). An account nobody wrote down is an orphan the owner discovers on a bill.
name: account_record

description: The account registry: every identity the project has created in the world. Read it before signing up anywhere (it may already exist) and when winding anything down.
name: accounts_list

description: Put a decision to the chairman as a recommendation you would defend — never an open question. kind: spend|legal|owner_decision|tool_request. Unanswered approvals expire to DENIED. An approval BLOCKS on a human, so it is the wrong tool for anything the constitution already put in your hands: where the authority dial grants you the plan, the scope and the date, an owner_decision is refused and names the verb to use instead. To want his opinion without blocking, use ask_chairman and keep going. He decides it cold, often from an email: title says what he is approving in plain words; body is what it is, why now, and the number that justifies it, with everything named by what it is rather than by an ID; if_declined is what happens if he says no or lets it expire — required, because on most projects that is the default.
name: approval_request

description: List this project's recent approvals and their status.
name: approvals_list

description: Read a shipped artifact's bytes back. ref is either a key from artifact_list or the uri cited in a message, evidence row, or task completion. Returns the whole file's size and sha256 plus a slice of its content (text when the file is text) — page a large file with offset, default 64 KB per read. An artifact uri is NOT a path in your sandbox; opening one with a file tool always fails. This is the only way to read what was actually shipped. exists:false means the uri was cited but no bytes are stored — that is a finding worth reporting, not an error on your part, and it costs you nothing to check.
name: artifact_get

description: List the deliverables this project has shipped to the artifact store: key, name, run_id, size, modified. Start here when checking anyone's work, including your own — the store is what shipped, the workspace is only what someone was working on, and the two can differ.
name: artifact_list

description: Persist a finished deliverable (report, dataset, document) to the platform's artifact store — the shipped, versioned record the platform serves and audits. A published file is how the chairman gets what he is paying for: no message or chat ceiling applies to it, so give him everything he needs to act, to check you and to decide. Ship it here and CITE it — never paste its contents into a channel or the boardroom. Your /workspace is NOT ephemeral: it persists with the project across runs and is shared by every agent on it, which makes it the right home for working state and cached data pulls; ship an artifact when the work is FINISHED. Pass path: a file under /workspace (absolute or workspace-relative) — the platform reads and uploads the bytes itself. NEVER base64-encode a file or route its contents through your own output to ship it; write it to the workspace and hand over the path. filename optionally renames the artifact (plain name, no path separators; defaults to the file's own name). content_base64 is a fallback for small payloads you have in hand and nowhere on disk; filename is required with it. Max 100 MB decoded either way. satisfies lists the requirement keys (R-03) this file delivers on. Returns the artifact's uri, key, size and sha256 — cite the uri in evidence, task completions and messages. The uri is NOT a path in your sandbox: read it back with artifact_get, never with a file tool.
name: artifact_put

description: Put a question to the chairman that your next move depends on. The reporting cadence does not hold this — a question is not a status. It does NOT block: keep working while you wait. answer_by_hours is when you stop waiting; default_action is exactly what you will do if he has not answered by then, and you are held to it, so write the real thing rather than 'decide later'. If the window passes you are woken to do it and to tell him you did. Use this instead of sitting on something he needs to see — a question nobody knows is waiting is how a project spends a day idle. He reads it cold, often from an email, so write each field for someone who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are (never an ID like R-07), numbers with what they compare to. title is the question in one line. body is what is going on. why is why it matters now, with the number that shows it — required. options (up to four, one line each, with the cost or effect of each) and recommendation (which you would pick and why) when there is a choice; leave both out for a plain question of fact.
name: ask_chairman

description: Close one of your questions by having acted on it and said so. message_id is the boardroom message where you told him what you did — with his answer, or with the default you named when its window passed. An ask does not close by going quiet.
name: ask_close

description: Any agent. A step only a HUMAN can do is blocking you — a captcha, a 2FA code, a KYC form, a signature, an account only the chairman can touch. Never try to defeat a security challenge; hand it over. Before calling: save your session state to the workspace (playwright storage_state / cookies, the URL you were on, what remains to do) — the workspace persists across runs, so the next run resumes where you stopped. Say exactly WHAT you need ('the 6-digit code SMS'd to your phone', 'solve the captcha at this URL and tell me done') and WHERE, naming the site and the account in full. It goes straight to the chairman, not through your team, and he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. His answer arrives verbatim in the decision that wakes you; unanswered it expires to no, so also plan the work that does not depend on it. If there is nothing for him to do ('no trade today, place nothing'), it is not an assist: a heads_up if a standing order asks him to be told, otherwise the deliverable carries it.
name: assist_request

description: Read the task board visible to you (open + recently closed).
name: board

description: CEO only. Write the chairman's CURRENT direction back to him for his Confirm: `goal` is the whole goal in plain words as it stands now (it replaces the old one, so write all of it, not a patch); `standing_orders` is every order in force, one sentence each WITH its number or value ('Max 15% of the book in one name', not 'keep positions sensible'); `retired` is what he has taken back, so agents that find it in a file or memory know it is dead; `what_changed` quotes what he said, with dates. Use it the moment he changes his mind about what the project is for, how it works, or any limit — agreeing in chat or saving a memory does NOT change what the other runs read. Nothing changes until he confirms; then every agent reads the new brief first on every run and you are told to rewrite the files, scripts and memories that still say the old thing. A new draft replaces any unconfirmed one. he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to.
name: brief_propose

description: CEO only. Put a case to the chairman for MORE of a capacity dial — runs a day, runs an hour, concurrency, queue depth, the month's money. This is the verb for the constraint that is actually binding: if you have worked out that the run ration is what paces you, say so here with the arithmetic rather than describing it in the boardroom, where it is a remark nobody can act on. rule is the constitution field; `to` is the number you want. All three of buys / costs / without are required and are the point — what more room BUYS in outcomes, what it COSTS in money and runs, and what happens WITHOUT it. A request without them is a wish, and he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. It does not block and filing it does not move the dial: keep working at the cap you have, plan for it, and treat a yes as upside — his yes is what raises it, and you are told the number in force. Unanswered it expires to no, which is the same as today. You may not request a lower bar, a change to who decides, or less auditing — those are his judgement about the project, not its throughput.
name: capacity_request

description: List your channels with unread counts.
name: channels

description: CEO only. Ask to commit to a delivery date. You do not and cannot write the date: the platform stamps its own projection from pace and scope, and the chairman accepts it (with that date or his own) or declines. Nothing binds until he does. The optional note travels with the proposal to him — what the date rests on; he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to.
name: commitment_propose

description: CEO only, and only where the constitution grants you commitment_authority. Reset a promise that has stopped holding to the platform's CURRENT projection. You still cannot write a date — the only date you can reset to is the arithmetic's, so this buys no slack the pace has not already spent. Refused while the promise still holds. Every reset is audited, disclosed to the chairman with a running count of how many times you have done it, and reversible by him; the reason is what he reads, and he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. Reach for it when the honest answer is that the date cannot hold; reach for cutting scope first when the honest answer is that the scope is too big.
name: commitment_reset

description: CEO only, and only where the constitution grants capability_authority: ceo — otherwise a 403 naming the paths (file a need, or the chairman's boardroom order as a directive). Delegate an existing credential across your team: add_roles / remove_roles by role slug, with a reason. The value never moves — only who receives it at run time. Audited and sent to the chairman with your reason — he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. Effective on each role's next run.
name: credential_scope

description: CEO only. The credential roster: every service credential the project holds and which roles receive it — names and scopes only, never values. Read it before filing a need (the capability may already exist) or delegating one.
name: credentials_list

description: Call a tool on one of your data sources and write the FULL result to a file in your workspace WITHOUT it passing through your context. This is how bulk data is handled: fetch once to disk, then process the file with code (python3 has pandas and duckdb) or with Read/Grep slices, and report only the aggregate. server: the data source name (see DATA SOURCES in your system prompt). tool: that source's tool name, with or without its mcp__<server>__ prefix — OMIT tool to list what the source offers (names, descriptions and input schemas), which is how you discover a source that is not mounted as tools of your own. arguments: that tool's arguments, verbatim — prefer its own filter, date-range or pagination arguments over fetching everything and trimming later. path: optional workspace-relative destination; pass a stable path when you want a cache you can reuse, else it defaults to data/<server>/<tool>-<timestamp>.json. Returns {path, bytes, sha256, lines, rows, preview} — the preview is the first 2 KB ONLY; the answer is in the file, not the preview. Any mcp__* tools you do have are for small lookups you will read in full; use this for anything larger. Your workspace persists across runs, so check for an existing file before fetching again, and leave the script that processed it behind for the next run. approval_id: only for a tool your source's allowlist refuses — file data_write_request first, wait to be woken with the decision, then pass the approved id here with the SAME arguments you had approved.
name: data_fetch

description: After a data_fetch spent an approval, file what the call DID — on the run that made it, or the next one once the effect can be read. ok: whether the call succeeded; observed: {label, value, basis, as_of} — the effect in the owner's numbers ('ad spend on the 14 terms', '$0 in the 7 days since', the window it covers); note: anything else he should know. Without this the owner sees 'approved · applied' and never learns whether it worked.
name: data_write_outcome

description: Ask the chairman to approve ONE call your data source's allowlist refuses — a change to his live account, not a read. Pass the arguments you intend to send, exactly: he decides on those, the platform records their fingerprint, and the approval is spendable on nothing else. Approved, it buys exactly one call — a second change needs a second approval, so batch with the tool's own bulk arguments rather than filing twenty requests. Say WHY in terms of what it does to his numbers, not what it does to your task — he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. Unanswered it expires to no; plan the work that does not need it. ALWAYS fill `disclosure` — it is what he decides on: `change_set` as [{entity, field, before, after}] for every thing that changes; `scope_counts` like {campaigns: 3, keywords: 14}; `evidence` as {columns, rows (the ones that matter, 200 at most), period_start, period_end, currency, as_of}; `estimate` as {label, value, basis} labelled as an estimate; `reversible` true/false; `counter_case` — the honest reason he might say no; `spend_affected_usd_month`; and `category` (one of: bids, budgets, targeting, negative_keywords, campaign_state, placements, other). A request without a disclosure is a paragraph with buttons.
name: data_write_request

description: Append to the decision record: what was decided and why.
name: decision_add

description: CEO: turn something the chairman said in the boardroom into something the platform does, citing the message he wrote it in. Two shapes, pass exactly one. `changes` files reporting policy the moment he changes how or how often he wants to be reported to — a rule kept in memory does not survive into the next run. Settable: chairman_report_interval_hours (0 disables), chairman_report_window_local ('09:00-20:00'), timezone (IANA name). `action` EXECUTES a plan order he gave — 'cut R-07', 'reopen R-04', 'move R-02 to stage 1', 'accept R-09', 'that estimate should be 12 runs', 'reword R-03 to …', 'R-05 should not wait on R-02' — as {"kind": "accept|cut|reopen|restage|reestimate|reword|unsequence", "requirement_key": "R-07", and for restage "stage", for reestimate "est_runs", for reword "statement", for unsequence "depends_on_key"}. It runs on HIS cited authority through the same machinery as his own buttons, and is echoed back to him threaded to his message, with your reason — he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. Use it the moment he gives an order instead of asking him to click it himself.
name: directive_file

description: List the environment variable NAMES available in your sandbox (never values). Answers 'do I have credential X?' definitively — use it instead of guessing.
name: env_list

description: Record evidence. kind='external' needs a source_url on a domain this project does NOT control; the platform fetches and verifies it before it counts. kind='internal' for everything we did to our own things.
name: evidence_add

description: Close a flag by having TOLD the chairman, with what you propose doing about it. Two steps, in this order: message_post the news in the boardroom, then flag_raise with that message_id — the message is the proof he was told, which is why saying it in the boardroom does not close the flag on its own and why nothing else can. flag_id comes from the flags in your context pack. The proposal is required: a flag without one is anxiety forwarded to his desk, and what you add over a monitoring alert is the sentence AFTER the bad news — what broke, the arithmetic, the ways out, the one you would pick, and what you need from him — and he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. Closing it dismissively is legitimate and expected: 'the cycle boundary caused it, no action needed' is this verb working exactly as intended. What is not available is leaving it open while telling him everything is fine.
name: flag_raise

description: The flags open on this project and whether each has been raised.
name: flags_list

description: CEO only. Tell the chairman something he ASKED to be told, for him to mark noted: tomorrow's ticket when it is 'no trade', the weekly number he wants to see. `standing_order` quotes the order in your brief that says to tell him — refused without one, because then it is information and belongs in the deliverable or the daily brief, not on his desk. No buttons to approve or deny and no expiry: if he must DECIDE, file an approval; if he must DO something, an assist. he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to.
name: heads_up

description: CEO only. Put a role on this project — yours to decide, no approval needed. `role_slug` comes from roles_list, `employees` are the names these people will work under, `reason` says what work this seat is for — it is posted to the boardroom for the chairman, and he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. Optionally set stand_down_when now, in the same shape stand_down_when takes. Hiring does not buy you runs: the daily ration and the monthly wall belong to the PROJECT, so another seat spreads the same allowance thinner and adds wake-ups of its own. Hire because work needs doing that nobody here can do, never because a seat would be nice to have.
name: hire

description: CEO: state a falsifiable bet with a dated kill condition (ISO datetime), written BEFORE the work starts.
name: hypothesis_add

description: CEO: kill a bet and say why.
name: hypothesis_kill

description: Your durable memory, in the standard memory-tool directory shape — over the SAME governed store as the memory_* tools, with the same rules (caps refuse adds; only a scope's curator edits, folds or deletes). Commands: view (path '/memories' lists entries; '/memories/<id>' shows one) · create (path '/memories/<scope>/<subject>.md' where scope is project|team, file_text is the content) · str_replace (path '/memories/<id>', old_str, new_str — edits one entry) · delete (path '/memories/<id>') · rename (path '/memories/<id>', new_path names the new subject). Check your memory directory at the start of a run; record only what will still be true next month.
name: memory

description: Write ONE durable fact/lesson/preference/contact that will still be true next month. Not a diary, and not a write-up: two or three sentences, because every memory you add is re-read by everyone who searches this scope for as long as it stands. If it needs more room than that it is a document — put it in a file and record the fact that the file exists. scope: 'project' (CEO only) or 'team'.
name: memory_add

description: Fold several overlapping memories into one (curators only) — the way to make room. Frees all but one of their slots; the originals stay readable via memory_search include_superseded=true, so folding is safe.
name: memory_compact

description: Forget a wrong/dead memory (curators only).
name: memory_forget

description: Search durable memory. Query it before repeating work. include_superseded=true also returns entries folded away by compaction.
name: memory_search

description: Replace ONE outdated memory with ONE new one (curators only). Frees no slot — use memory_compact or memory_forget for room.
name: memory_supersede

description: Post to one of your channels. THREE SENTENCES. Lead with the answer or the ask, add the number that carries it, stop — no narration of what you did or decided, which the board and your memory already hold. Anything that genuinely needs more room goes in a file or a task, and you post the line that points at it: this body is re-read by every recipient on every wake, a file is read once by whoever needs it. Boardroom: CEO<->chairman, and he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. Leadership: CEO+leads. Team room: your team. Use thread_id to reply in a thread. An unprompted boardroom status is refused between the chairman's cadence slots (see the `chairman` block in your context); set override to 'blocker', 'budget' or 'approval' only when it truly cannot wait — overrides are recorded and he sees them. Asking him something is NOT a status and is not an override: that is ask_chairman, which this gate has never held.
name: message_post

description: Read recent messages in one of your channels (advances your cursor).
name: messages_read

description: CEO only. File a NEED with the chairman: a capability the project lacks — 'I need AWS access, give me a key', 'we need a Stripe account', 'SMTP credentials for the writer'. It reaches him where he reads (boardroom, Slack, email) and he fulfills it in one motion: the credential lands as an env var for the roles you name, and you are woken with the decision. Unanswered, it expires to no — plan the work that does not depend on it rather than waiting. Say WHY (what work it unblocks), suggest a credential name, name the roles, and estimate monthly cost honestly. The title and why are what he reads; he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to.
name: need_request

description: CEO only. Answer a note the chairman wrote on a decision (your context's chairman_notes lists every unanswered one, every run, until you do). `reply` is one line he reads under his note: what you did with it. `standing` says whether it applies beyond that one item. A standing note belongs in the brief: call brief_propose with it folded in FIRST, or the answer is refused. Never answer one by saving a memory.
name: note_answer

description: Clear a real-world purchase against the spend envelope BEFORE paying — a refusal here costs nothing; the same refusal after paying costs the money. Records the purchase with a stable idempotency_key so a crash or retry can never buy twice: if the response says duplicate/completed, the money already moved — do NOT pay again. Then pay with whatever tool fits (the platform never holds the card for you), and call purchase_finish with the receipt. usd over the per-purchase line or the approval threshold needs an approved approval_id; the monthly external cap is a wall no approval overrides — recommend an amendment instead.
name: purchase_begin

description: Close a purchase opened with purchase_begin. ok=true books the ledger entry and keeps the receipt (quote the vendor's own confirmation — what was bought, from whom, for how much); ok=false records the failure and books nothing. Finishing twice never double-books.
name: purchase_finish

description: CEO only. Bring a stood-down role back, with its channel, memory and history intact — cheaper and better than hiring a replacement. A seat the CHAIRMAN paused is not yours to recall. The reason is posted to the boardroom for the chairman, and he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to.
name: recall

description: CEO only. Record that one requirement cannot be worked until another is settled. This is the sequencing the chairman looks at, and it is enforced: work is refused for a requirement whose dependencies are still open. An edge that would close a loop is refused.
name: requirement_depends_on

description: CEO only. Propose something that must be TRUE at the end — not a task, an outcome. acceptance_test has the same shape as a success test: {"type":"command","command":...} the platform runs itself, {"type":"observable","target":...} the chairman confirms, or {"type":"metric","source":{"kind":"http_json","url":...,"path":"$.a.b[-1].c"},"direction":"decreasing","target":500000,"measure_every_hours":24} the platform MEASURES on a schedule. If this requirement is the objective itself — the rank, the revenue, the number the project exists to move — it is a metric, and nothing else will do: a command greps a file you wrote, so a finish line you can write into your own status report is not a finish line. Use a command for work that must be verifiably done, and an observable only when neither fits — it puts the chairman in the loop every time it closes, and a metric never does, because the platform reads the number itself. This is a PROPOSAL and creates no scope — the chairman accepts it, and until he does no work may be created for it. You cannot accept your own, and you cannot mark one met: the platform runs the test and writes the result. stage is the order this happens in (1, 2, 3…); est_runs is your honest guess at how many runs it will take, and it is compared against what it actually costs. depends_on lists requirement ids that must be settled first. recurrence is 'terminal' (met once) or 'standing' (owed again every cycle; Operate only). ALWAYS fill meta — it is what the project's OWNER sees: {title: a noun they want ('Wasted-spend list'), description: one line of what they get in spreadsheet terms, cadence: daily|weekly|null, due: an ISO date or null, lands: report|memo|note|table}. The statement is for the platform; meta is for the person who hired you.
name: requirement_propose

description: CEO only, when a review is open (see the `review` block in your context). File your variance narrative for the standing status meeting: what moved against the plan since the last review, the SINGLE largest cause named (a piece of work, a bet that failed, a run of failures — named by what it is, not by its key), and in `recommended`, what you would cut or move. The platform's numbers are already on the review — explain them, do not restate them. The chairman reads this at the meeting, and he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. His decisions come back to you as notices with his reasons.
name: review_narrative

description: CEO only. The role library you may hire from — slug, name, category and what the role is for, plus which roles are already on your roster and how many teams you may run. Read it before hiring: the seat you want may already be here under a different team name.
name: roles_list

description: Who spent the runs, and on what. `since` takes 'today' (the default), 'yesterday', '7d', '12h', a date like 2026-09-12, or an ISO timestamp; 'today' means today in the project's timezone, not a rolling 24 hours. Per seat you get runs split by kind and by outcome, what woke each one, tokens, money, tasks claimed and completed, and what they are holding now. READ THIS BEFORE YOU ANSWER ANY QUESTION ABOUT WHO SPENT WHAT. Do not estimate from what you remember doing: the last CEO asked 'who did today's 15 runs' guessed six of them were its own and had spent twelve, while asking for a bigger ration on the strength of the guess. `died_of` is why the dead runs died — the cause in words, the tokens it cost, and `produced_work_first`, the number of them that had already claimed a task or filed work before they were cut. NEVER read a dead run as an idle one without checking that number: a CEO reported eleven runs that 'died without finishing anything' and moved to stand the seat down; seven of the eleven had filed work, every task that seat touched completed on a retry, and the real fault was a ceiling cutting it off mid-task. Fix the cause before you blame the seat.
name: roster_activity

description: CEO only, and only where the constitution's authority dial grants it (your constitution prose says which verbs you hold; everything you don't hold is a 403 with the legitimate path named). Exercise a scope verb as YOUR OWN authority: {"kind": "accept|cut|reopen|restage|reestimate|reword|unsequence|verdict", "requirement_key": "R-07", plus for restage "stage", for reestimate "est_runs", for reword "statement", for unsequence "depends_on_key", for verdict "ok" (bool)}. verdict is for an UNVERIFIABLE observable in checking — judge it honestly and keep going; every self-judgment is disclosed to the chairman in full. Every use is audited and sent to the chairman with your reason — he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to. All of it is reversible. Spend this authority the way you would want it audited. This is not the tool for executing a chairman boardroom order — that is directive_file, citing his message, and works in every mode.
name: scope_act

description: REQUIRED before any external side effect (posting, emailing, spending, creating a PR): record it with a stable idempotency_key. If the response says duplicate/completed, DO NOT fire the effect again — a prior attempt already did.
name: side_effect_begin

description: Mark a recorded side effect completed/failed with its result.
name: side_effect_finish

description: Book a real-world dollar spend you made with your own tooling. Every spend faces the same envelope as purchase_begin: the monthly external cap is a hard wall, and amounts over the per-purchase line or the approval threshold need an approved approval_id. For a purchase you are ABOUT to make, prefer purchase_begin/purchase_finish — it checks the envelope before money moves and books itself. Every real purchase gets booked, one way or the other: an unbooked spend is what the chairman's spot-audit exists to catch.
name: spend_book

description: CEO only. Stop a role whose job is finished — yours to decide, no approval needed. Its seats stop waking, stop reading, and stop costing; the team's channel, memory and history all stay. THIS IS NOT A PAUSE and it is not a punishment: it is the normal end of a role that was needed for the front half of a project. An idle seat is not free — it wakes to read its channels and it counts as a mover in your capacity forecast. Refused if the team is holding open work (finish it, kill it or move it first) and refused for your last challenge seat, which is not yours to remove. The reason is posted to the boardroom for the chairman, and he reads it cold, so write it for a person who has not opened the project: plain words, things named by what they are rather than by an ID, numbers with what they compare to.
name: stand_down

description: CEO only. Say NOW when a team's job will end, and the platform will stand it down itself when that comes true. Two shapes: {"kind": "requirement_met", "keys": ["R-03"]} stops the seat once those requirements are all settled, and {"kind": "stage_cleared", "stage": 2} stops it once every requirement at or below that stage has settled. SET THIS FOR EVERY TEAM WHILE YOU ARE WRITING THE PLAN. Writing the plan is the one moment you know which roles are for the front half of this project — the requirements gathering, the build, the validation — and it is the moment nobody has ever asked you. Afterwards nothing raises the question and an idle seat costs quietly. Pass when: null to clear one.

description: Block your claimed task with a reason; the CEO will re-plan.

description: Claim a ready task that is yours to work.

description: Complete your claimed task with observed evidence (what you ran/saw, quoted). Command-type success tests are then executed by the platform, not by you.

description: Create a task. CEO only for team tasks; team leads create subtasks (assignments) under a team task they claimed. success_test must be {"type":"command","command":...} (platform-executed) or {"type":"observable","target":...}. assignee_agent_id IS ONLY FOR SUBTASKS. A team task names a TEAM, never a person: the team's lead claims it and decides who does what. Setting assignee_agent_id without parent_task_id is refused every time — it is the single most common refusal on this platform, so check yourself before you send it. A team task OMITS parent_task_id, assignee_agent_id and hypothesis_id entirely — never send 'null' or '""' as a placeholder, it is read as an id and refused. not_before is an ISO 8601 datetime before which the task cannot be claimed. It wakes nobody and shows on no screen as work in progress, so a project gated on one looks stopped: use it only for a genuine calendar rhythm, never to express 'after the other task finishes'. For that, create this task WHEN that one lands — you are woken for it. Gates beyond the constitution's limit are refused. requirement_id names what this work is FOR and is required outside Explore projects: a task that serves no requirement is refused, because work that makes nothing true is how a project stays busy without finishing. Your context pack's `board` and `roster` carry the team ids, agent ids and requirement ids you need — read them rather than guessing at an id.
name: task_create

description: Kill a task (CEO for team tasks; lead for own subtasks).

description: Sign off, or send back, work somebody else finished and left waiting for a read. `ok` true closes it; false returns it to whoever wrote it with your notes. Say what is ABSENT and which standard it fails — returning work is ordinary here, not an escalation, and 'looks fine' teaches the writer nothing. You cannot review your own work.
